analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for the costliest brand-name drugs and caps seniors' drug costs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 92 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Medicare is prohibited from negotiating drug prices. This bill would require the government to negotiate maximum prices for the costliest single-source brand-name drugs — at least 25 in the first year and at least 50 per year after that, plus insulin products — capping them at 120% of the average price in six other wealthy countries. It would also charge manufacturers rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation, cap seniors' yearly out-of-pocket drug costs, and fund opioid response and medical research.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare enrollees, who would pay less for the most expensive brand-name drugs and face a hard cap on annual out-of-pocket drug spending. People with private insurance would also get access to the negotiated maximum price unless their plan opts out, and taxpayers would save as Medicare stopped paying prices far above what other countries pay.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to negotiate maximum prices for single-source brand-name drugs among the 125 costliest nationally or under Medicare — at least 25 drugs for 2024 and at least 50 thereafter, plus insulin products and certain newly approved drugs.

Caps the negotiated price at 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom, or 85% of the U.S. average manufacturer price where international data is unavailable.
Applies the negotiated maximum price to Medicare and lets group health plans and private insurers participate unless they affirmatively opt out, with nonparticipants publicly disclosed.
Requires manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare for covered drugs costing $100 or more whose average price rises faster than inflation.
Caps annual out-of-pocket spending under the Medicare Part D prescription drug benefit and funds opioid epidemic initiatives and NIH and FDA research.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers: their prices for the costliest drugs would be capped against international benchmarks, they would owe inflation rebates on Medicare drugs, and a manufacturer that refuses to negotiate faces an excise tax rising from 65% to 95% of sales plus civil penalties up to ten times the overcharge per violation.

drawbacks.text: The program covers only the very costliest drugs — the top 125 by spending, with at least 25 selected in 2024 and 50 per year after — leaving the large majority of prescription drugs outside the negotiation program.

Prices are capped at 120% of prices in six peer countries and refusing manufacturers face an excise tax rising to 95% of sales; an honest supporter has to acknowledge the argument that squeezing revenue this hard on top-selling drugs could reduce the industry's investment in developing future medicines.

Private insurers can opt out of offering the negotiated maximum price for any selected drug, so privately insured patients would get the lower price automatically only where their plan chooses not to opt out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to Medicare enrollees, privately insured patients, and taxpayers are large and direct — negotiated prices on the drugs that drive U.S. spending, an inflation rebate, and a hard out-of-pocket cap for seniors. The main cost falls on a single concentrated industry, and the strongest objection — possible slower development of new drugs — is a real but hard-to-quantify tradeoff that the bill partially addresses by prioritizing R&D costs and therapeutic advance in the negotiation factors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to five House committees the day it was introduced, and no committee ever marked it up and no chamber ever voted on it, so it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 22, 2021 and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, and Veterans' Affairs committees and to subcommittees.
Gained 92 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, while Democrats held the House majority.
No further action of any kind appears in the record after the early subcommittee referrals — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they kept the ability to set prices without government negotiation, avoided the inflation rebates and out-of-pocket cap, and faced no excise tax. Patients and taxpayers continued paying U.S. prices that run well above those in other wealthy countries.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Lead sponsor; Chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it to committee referral in his own chamber.

for.name: Richard Neal and Bobby Scott
for.role: Original cosponsors; Chairmen of Ways and Means and of Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction, putting the chairs of two committees with jurisdiction behind it.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor calendar and never scheduled the bill for a vote; it sat at the referral stage for the entire Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill or moved a companion through the Senate; no Senate action appears in the record.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug makers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign against government price negotiation throughout the debate over drug pricing legislation in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 92 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor or recorded action appears for the bill; with Democrats holding both the House majority and the Senate, the bill still never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Their prices on the costliest drugs would be capped at 120% of international benchmarks, they would owe inflation rebates on Medicare drugs, and refusing to negotiate would trigger an excise tax climbing to 95% of sales. The savings paying for lower senior drug costs and a hard out-of-pocket cap come directly out of their revenue.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug intermediaries
industries.note: The inflation rebates and the requirement that the negotiated maximum price be applied at the pharmacy counter shrink the gap between list prices and net prices that intermediaries profit from.
Plans that participate pay the negotiated maximum price on covered selected drugs, lowering their drug costs; insurers could also opt out drug by drug, and nonparticipants must be publicly listed.
